newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Amnesty fears rights erosion in Hong Kong.
newsitem.headline: Amnesty fears rights erosion in Hong Kong.

text.p: Human rights watchdog Amnesty International said on Wednesday it was concerned about the future of civil rights and freedoms in Hong Kong after the British colony reverts to Chinese rule on July 1.
It its 1997 annual report, extracts of which were made available to the media, it said its fears were reinforced by plans in Hong Kong to change safeguards to human rights.

"Amnesty International remained concerned that the right to freedom of expression and association could be severely curtailed in Hong Kong following its return to Chinese sovereignty in 1997, particularly in the light of proposals to change human rights safeguards," the London-based human rights group said.

The proposals refer to laws passed last week by a China-backed interim legislature which will ban foreign funding for Hong Kong political groups and require people to apply for permits before they can hold demonstrations.
The lawmaking chamber, formed under Beijing's auspices in December, will be installed in Hong Kong at the handover, replacing the current elected Legislative Council.

The report also gave details of human rights abuses in 150 other countries and territories and said serious human rights violations were committed in "virtually every country of the Asia Pacific region during 1996".

In Sri Lanka, it said "disappearances" hit the highest level since 1992 because of hostility between the government and the rebel Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam. It said it had documented more than 220 cases, mostly in the northern Jaffna peninsula. It also criticised government crackdowns on pro-democracy activists in Indonesia and Burma. In Indonesia, members of unofficial opposition parties and trade unionists were detained and were now facing unfair trials for subversion, Amnesty said.
India, Pakistan and Cambodia were also highlighted in the report for violence against journalists.
In some areas of Afghanistan, women and girls were beaten with chains for simply straying outside their homes, Amnesty said.
China's long-drawn war against crime, or the "Strike Hard" campaign, had seen at least 6,000 people sentenced to death in 1996, with at least 3,500 already executed, it said.
